title: 📈 ICP Waveform
text: Waveforms often change BEFORE ICP rises → early warning system.

title: 📈 ICP Waveform
text:
Normal ICP Waveform

Normal: P1 > P2 > P3 → intact intracranial compliance.

P1: Arterial pulsation
P2: Brain compliance
P3: Venous outflow

Takeaway: P2 should NEVER exceed P1.

title: 📈 ICP Waveform
text:
Abnormal ICP Waveform

Abnormal: P2 > P1 → reduced intracranial compliance.

Early intracranial hypertension
Loss of compensatory reserve
Precedes ICP elevation







Warning



Early Warning: Waveform changes occur BEFORE ICP rises.

title: 📈 ICP Waveform
text:
How to Examine ICP Waveform
Watch how to interpret ICP waveform at the bedside:







Tip



Think: Is P2 higher than P1? What does that imply about compliance?

title: ⚠️ Transport ICP Risk
text:
Clinical Scenario
A neurocritical care patient with a clamped EVD is being transported for imaging.
Could transport increase the risk of ICP elevation?
This educational model explores factors associated with transport-related ICP elevation described in retrospective literature.

title: ⚠️ Transport ICP Risk
text:
Factors Associated with ICP Elevation

Higher baseline ICP
Higher CSF output
Early ICU phase
Unplanned transport
Longer transport duration

Educational model inspired by retrospective literature on transport-associated ICP elevation with clamped EVDs.

title: ⚠️ Transport ICP Risk

⚠️ Transport ICP Risk
text:
Potential Mitigation Strategies

Conduct multidisciplinary huddle.
Reassess urgency of transport.
Optimize sedation before transport.
Review EVD clamp strategy.
Minimize transport duration.
Ensure ICP monitoring preparedness.
Clarify roles before transport.
Re-level immediately after transport.

title: ⚠️ Transport ICP Risk
text:
Disclaimer






Warning



This educational model is hypothetical and intended for awareness, simulation-based learning, and educational purposes only. The transport-associated ICP risk model has not been prospectively validated and should not be used as a clinical decision-making tool. This tool is intended to promote awareness surrounding transport-associated ICP elevation and multidisciplinary transport preparedness. Clinical decisions should always rely on institutional protocols, multidisciplinary communication, bedside assessment, and clinician judgment.

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text: The EVD setting represents the pressure threshold (cm H₂O) above which CSF will drain.

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
The Three Common Settings






Note5 cm H₂O — Aggressive drainage



Used in patients with unresolved hydrocephalus or with low ICPs to facilitate CSF drainage.








Note10 cm H₂O — Moderate drainage



Commonly used after a ruptured aneurysm has been secured. Institutional practices may vary on the setting — please correlate with your institution’s practice.








Note20 cm H₂O — Restricted drainage



Prevents overdrainage before an aneurysm is secured.

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
Clinical Model

EVD behaves like a pressure-regulated valve
ICP must exceed the setting for drainage
Setting, ICP, and CSF output are interdependent







Tip



Clinical Pearl: Always interpret ICP in the context of the EVD setting.

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
CSF Output (mL/hr)

High output → low setting OR elevated ICP
Low output → high setting, low ICP, or obstruction
Trend matters more than single values

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
Clamp Status

Open: CSF drains if ICP exceeds setting
Clamped: No drainage → ICP reflects true pressure







Warning



Critical: Interpretation changes completely when the EVD is clamped.

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
Leveling

Reference point = external auditory meatus
Small height errors → large pressure errors
Always confirm before interpreting ICP

title: 🎚️ EVD Settings
text:
Common Errors

Ignoring EVD setting
Not checking clamp status
Misinterpreting CSF output
Failure to confirm leveling

text: A quick-reference guide to safe, high-quality care when managing external ventricular drains.

title: ☑️ Best Practices
text:
Do’s and Don’ts







Do
Don’t




✔ Confirm EVD setting before interpreting ICP
✖ Interpret ICP without knowing the drain setting


✔ Check clamp status before transport or procedures
✖ Keep EVD closed and not monitor ICP


✔ Level the transducer at the external auditory meatus
✖ Clamp EVD and leave the transducer at the level of the heart


✔ Trend ICP and waveform together
✖ Rely on a single ICP value


✔ Minimize CSF system access
✖ Access CSF unnecessarily


✔ Use sterile technique for all handling
✖ Break sterility during manipulation


✔ Secure tubing to prevent dislodgement
✖ Leave tubing unsecured


✔ Communicate EVD status during handoffs
✖ Assume others know the EVD setup


✔ Monitor ICP during transport at all times
✖ Transport without considering ICP risk


✔ Reassess waveform if values seem inconsistent
✖ Ignore dampened or abnormal waveforms

title: ☑️ Best Practices
text:
CSF Color Interpretation







CSF Appearance
Clinical Interpretation




Clear
Normal CSF


Xanthochromia (yellow)
Suggests prior hemorrhage or SAH breakdown products


Bloody
May indicate active bleeding, traumatic tap, or evolving hemorrhage


Cloudy
Concerning for infection (e.g., ventriculitis)


Debris / Particulate
Possible clot breakdown, infection, or catheter obstruction









Warning



Clinical Note: Changes in CSF color should always be interpreted in clinical context and may warrant further evaluation.

title: ☑️ Best Practices
text:
Key Takeaway






Tip



Clinical Pearl: Most EVD-related errors are system-based (leveling, clamping, interpretation). A structured approach prevents harm.

title: 🩺 Apply to a Hypothetical Patient
section: What has been described in the literature?
text:
What has been described in the literature?
Retrospective analyses have identified factors associated with ICP elevation ≥20 mmHg during transport when EVDs are clamped (Chaikittisilpa et al., 2017).






Important




Higher baseline ICP
Higher CSF output
EVD open prior to transport
Unplanned/emergent transport
Early ICU phase



These findings are derived from: Chaikittisilpa N, Lele AV, Lyons VH, Nair BG, Newman SF, Blissitt PA, Vavilala MS. Risks of Routinely Clamping External Ventricular Drains for Intrahospital Transport in Neurocritically Ill Cerebrovascular Patients. Neurocrit Care. 2017;26(2):196–204.

title: 🩺 Apply to a Hypothetical Patient
text:
Exploratory Risk Model
Estimates probability of ICP elevation ≥20 mmHg during transport (derived from Chaikittisilpa et al., 2017).

viewof icp = Inputs.select(["<15", "15–19", "≥20"], {label: "Baseline ICP"})
viewof intubated = Inputs.select(["Yes", "No"], {label: "Intubated"})
viewof duration = Inputs.range([0, 120], {label: "Transport Time (min)", step: 1, value: 30})
viewof days = Inputs.range([0, 30], {label: "ICU Day", step: 1, value: 5})
viewof csf = Inputs.number({label: "CSF Output (mL/hr)", value: 5})
viewof iht = Inputs.select(["Therapeutic", "Diagnostic"], {label: "Transport Type"})
viewof unscheduled = Inputs.select(["Yes", "No"], {label: "Unplanned"})



















































risk_icp = icp === "<15" ? 1 : icp === "15–19" ? 3.4 : 12.94
risk_intubated = intubated === "Yes" ? 0.58 : 1
risk_duration = (duration / 10) * 0.95
risk_days = days * 0.97
risk_csf = csf * 1.11
risk_iht = iht === "Therapeutic" ? 5.82 : 1
risk_unscheduled = unscheduled === "Yes" ? 1.2 : 1

risk = risk_icp * risk_intubated * risk_duration * risk_days * risk_csf * risk_iht * risk_unscheduled * 0.118
result = Math.round(Math.min(risk, 100) * 10) / 10

category = result < 20 ? "LOW RISK" : result < 50 ? "MODERATE RISK" : "HIGH RISK"
color = result < 20 ? "#2ecc71" : result < 50 ? "#f39c12" : "#e74c3c"















































































html`<div style="padding:18px;border-radius:12px;background:${color};color:white;font-size:18px;text-align:center;">
  <strong>${category}</strong><br>
  ${result}% probability of ICP ≥20 mmHg
</div>`












TipWhat does this mean?





This model estimates the probability of ICP elevation ≥20 mmHg during transport with a clamped EVD, derived from retrospective data in Chaikittisilpa et al., 2017.

Low Risk: minimal signal
Moderate Risk: consider mitigation strategies
High Risk: strong signal → reassess transport plan

Not prospectively validated. For educational use only.

title: 🧠 What is an EVD
text:
An External Ventricular Drain (EVD) is a temporary device inserted into the ventricular system to allow controlled drainage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and monitoring of intracranial pressure (ICP).
It is primarily used for temporary CSF diversion in patients with acute symptomatic hydrocephalus.

title: 🧠 What is an EVD
text:
An External Ventricular Drain (EVD) is a temporary device inserted into the ventricular system to allow controlled drainage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and monitoring of intracranial pressure (ICP).
It is primarily used for temporary CSF diversion in patients with acute symptomatic hydrocephalus.

title: 🧠 What is an EVD
text:
Common Indications

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)
Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH)
Traumatic brain injury with hydrocephalus
Posterior fossa lesions causing obstruction
CNS infections with hydrocephalus

title: 🧠 What is an EVD
text:
CT Abnormalities






NoteCisternal blood (Basilar aneurysm rupture)






Cisternal blood due to ruptured basilar aneurysm causing obstruction of CSF pathways.
Source: Dr. Abhijit V. Lele, University of Washington.









NoteIntracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular extension






Thalamic hemorrhage with intraventricular extension and hydrocephalus.
Source: Dr. Abhijit V. Lele, University of Washington.









NoteCerebellar ischemic stroke with edema






Cerebellar ischemic stroke with posterior fossa edema causing compression of the fourth ventricle.
Source: Dr. Abhijit V. Lele, University of Washington.

title: 🧠 What is an EVD
text:
Clinical Pearls

Leveling matters: Always level the EVD at the external auditory meatus for accurate ICP measurement.
Drain vs monitor: An open EVD prioritizes CSF drainage; a clamped EVD allows accurate ICP monitoring.
Transport risk: Clamping an EVD during transport can lead to dangerous ICP elevations.
Output trends: A sudden drop in CSF output may indicate obstruction rather than improvement.
Infection prevention: Maintain a closed system and minimize unnecessary access to reduce infection risk.

title: 🛡️ Infection Prevention Bundle
text: A structured, evidence-informed approach to reduce ventriculostomy-related infections (VRI) through standardized insertion and maintenance practices.

title: 🛡️ Infection Prevention Bundle
text:
Insertion Bundle
Definition: Number of patients with EVDs for whom all elements of an insertion bundle are documented at the time of EVD placement.
Core Elements:

🧼 Use of strict sterile technique during insertion
💉 Administration of periprocedural antibiotics prior to incision
🧪 Use of antimicrobial-impregnated catheter
📏 Tunneling of the catheter (≥ 5 cm under the skin)
🔒 Use of a closed drainage system
🩹 Application of a sterile (preferably chlorhexidine-impregnated) dressing







Tip



Key Principle: Full compliance with all bundle elements—not partial adherence—is required to meaningfully reduce infection risk.

title: 🛡️ Infection Prevention Bundle
text:
Maintenance Bundle
Core Principles:

🧠 Indication-based CSF sampling only
🚫 Avoid routine or unnecessary CSF sampling
🔒 Minimize system access to prevent contamination
📐 Maintain system upright to prevent backflow
⚠️ Prevent accidental disconnection of the system







Tip



Key Principle: Each access of the CSF system increases infection risk—minimize manipulation unless clinically indicated.

title: 🛡️ Infection Prevention Bundle
text:
Why This Matters
Ventriculostomy-related infections are associated with increased morbidity, prolonged hospital stay, and higher healthcare costs. Standardizing insertion and maintenance practices reduces variability and improves patient outcomes.






Warning



Clinical Reminder: Infection prevention is a multidisciplinary responsibility involving anesthesia, neurosurgery, nursing, and ICU teams.

title: 🛡️ EVD Safety Campaign
text:
About the Campaign
The EVD Safety Campaign is an international educational and quality improvement initiative from the Society for Neuroscience in Anesthesiology and Critical Care (SNACC) focused on improving the safety of external ventricular drain (EVD) management across perioperative and neurocritical care environments.
The campaign emphasizes:

Education
Standardization
Transport safety
ICP monitoring awareness
Multidisciplinary collaboration
Prevention of avoidable complications







Tip



SNACC EVD Safety Campaign — visit the official SNACC EVD Safety Campaign website to access educational resources, publications, and collaborative initiatives.
Open SNACC Campaign Website →



Campaign Participation
Institutions, clinicians, trainees, nurses, APPs, educators, anesthesiology teams, and neurocritical care professionals worldwide are encouraged to participate in the EVD Safety Campaign.
Participating institutions may be highlighted on the campaign outreach map to showcase international collaboration and commitment to EVD safety.
Participation may include:

Educational initiatives
Simulation training
Local QI projects
EVD safety protocols
Transport safety workflows
Campaign collaboration

title: 🛡️ EVD Safety Campaign
text:
Endorsements
Supporting organizations and collaborators
The EVD Safety Campaign has been supported through multidisciplinary collaboration involving neurocritical care, anesthesiology, perioperative safety, and quality improvement leaders.
Key collaborations include:

Society for Neuroscience in Anesthesiology and Critical Care (SNACC)
Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation (APSF)


Global Participation
The campaign continues to expand through international engagement and multidisciplinary collaboration focused on improving EVD safety worldwide. Currently more than 50 hospitals from more than 30 countries are part of the EVD Safety Campaign.

title: 🛡️ EVD Safety Campaign
text:
Global Outreach
International collaboration and participation
The EVD Safety Campaign continues to expand through multidisciplinary international collaboration involving anesthesiology, neurocritical care, nursing, trainees, APPs, educators, and quality improvement leaders.
Participating institutions across the world are contributing to educational outreach, EVD safety awareness, and implementation of quality improvement initiatives.






Tip

Campaign Outreach Goals

Promote international EVD safety awareness
Advance multidisciplinary education
Share institutional best practices
Improve transport preparedness
Reduce preventable EVD complications
Build a collaborative neurocritical care community
